title: Do you bother paying for 3D assets when your game is still mostly placeholders?
author: No-Training-6156
selftext:
I'm still at the stage where half the stuff in my game could get deleted next week. Spending money on nicely textured props feels a little early when I'm not even sure the level is going to stay.

But I also don't want to spend hours making every random bit of scenery in Blender. So I want to know what you can actually get out of free AI 3D tools. Using Meshy as example because its free plan has a distinction that's easy to miss: having credits to generate something doesn't necessarily mean you can download it.

For a basic prop, this is the route I'd take:

Start with Text to 3D, or Image to 3D if there's already a reference.

Pick Meshy 6 Lite before generating and leave textures off. Check the credit cost shown before running it.

Once the model is generated, inspect the mesh and grab the file through Download. Then bring it into the game engine and check the scale, geometry and how it looks in the actual scene.

The free plan gives you 100 credits per month, and Meshy 6 Lite generation currently costs 10 credits. But the download limit is separate: 10 downloads per month, only for untextured Meshy 6 Lite models.

Generate something with Meshy 6, 7 or T2.5, or texture the model afterward, and those free downloads won't cover it. Buying more credits doesn't unlock the paid download options either.

There's also the license to remember. Free-plan models are under CC BY 4.0, so if one ends up in a released game, Meshy needs to be credited.

For background props that might get replaced anyway, plain meshes seem perfectly reasonable. I'd rather spend time making the gameplay work first.

Characters, important props, or anything that needs a consistent art style? Different story. At some point the cleanup and reworking can take longer than just making or buying something suitable.

How early do you start spending money on proper game assets? Still using placeholder cubes until the mechanics work, or sorting out the art as you go?

comments.author: frankenstein-0x00e
comments.body:
Just rawdogging it with Claude X Blender X I draw objects in paint and talk with claude to make them in blender

  
it keeps them interesting and I keep my assets half cooked to be open to artstyles 

  
Meshy AI is not the best option unless you are doing small objects which you need to clean up, the thing is, it serves to you in a golden plate, you have to eat up whatever it gives and it slowly takes over your art style and your game loses its feel

  
I think (not promoting) buying $200 Claude plan and have a lot of patience with it you will get there.

Here is the latest 3D thing I made with claude, its based on a reference so there is that but now I can adjust however I like 

Don't copy references, learn from them complex shapes so Claude can reuse these tools / workflows in different objects :3 

anyway sorry for yap, I just think text to 3D models still need 6 to 12 months before they become "game ready asset generators"

dont worry early on about assets or details, focus on how the game feels, if you game feels shitty with basic assets, it will feel ✨ shitty ✨ with high quality assets

comments.author: RegioMamalon666
comments.body:
I use AI mostly to code my game and a bit of blender mcp but I have been making games as a hobby for a while now so I already have gigs of nice 3d assets, it would be a fool not to use them.

The thing is, I do strip them away from textures on the first prorotype versions, and I do not use many of them, the goal initially is to add some props that would help define level layouts or give a specific vibe.

I love this step because it forces you to go minimal but with a goal, like, if I'm working on a swamp what are the minimal props that would give off that vibe, or if I need some platforming obstacles which ones do fit the over all level layout or goal.
